definitions.meaning: A function F with F'(x) = f(x): it undoes differentiation, so the antiderivative of 2x is x^2 + C.
The accumulation of a quantity under a curve; finding it is integration, the reverse process of differentiation.
The exact accumulated area under a curve between two bounds a and b, written as the integral from a to b, and computed as F(b) - F(a).
The +C in an indefinite integral: every vertical shift of an antiderivative has the same derivative, so the whole family is named by adding C.
An integral with no bounds: it names the whole family of antiderivatives, so it must always include the constant of integration.
An estimate of the area under a curve made by adding the areas of rectangles; as the rectangles get thinner, the sum converges on the definite integral.

mechanismSteps: The antiderivative is accumulated area - as x sweeps right, shaded strips pile up under the curve, and the antiderivative at each x is exactly that accumulated area.
Riemann sum: thin rectangles converge on the area - add the areas of wide rectangles for a rough total, then halve the widths and double the count until the sum closes in on the exact area.
Worked: evaluating a definite integral - antidifferentiate, evaluate the antiderivative at the upper and lower bounds, and subtract: upper minus lower.
Misconception: never drop the +C - x^2, x^2 + 5 and x^2 - 3 all have derivative 2x, so the indefinite integral of 2x is the whole family x^2 + C.
objectives: Explain the antiderivative as accumulated area under a curve
Use Riemann sums to see the definite integral as the limit of rectangle areas
Evaluate a definite integral by antidifferentiating and subtracting the bounds, and include +C in every indefinite integral
subject: math
title: A-Math integration: area, accumulation and the +C trap

trap.explanation: The slip: The constant term is forgotten. The fix: Never drop the +C: differentiating x^2 + 5 and x^2 + 7 both give 2x. So the integral of 2x is x^2 + C, not x^2 alone.

workedExample: Evaluate the definite integral step by step (s3). Step 1: integrate 2x from 1 to 2 by antidifferentiating: the antiderivative x^2. Step 2: evaluate the antiderivative at the upper bound: at x = 2, x^2 = 4. Step 3: evaluate at the lower bound: at x = 1, x^2 = 1. Step 4: subtract, upper minus lower: 4 - 1 = 3, so the area under y = 2x from 1 to 2 is 3 square units. Note that no +C appears: the constant would cancel in the subtraction.
